$comment: THE CATALOGUE. Single source of truth for everything the Android shell can do for a page. Everything else is generated from it: the runtime facade's action table, the gate mocks, the permission enum, the Java dispatch registry (phase 3), and the docs. Hand-writing any of those is how the two sides drift. See docs/research/apk-sdk-plan.md.

actions.summary: What the shell is and what it runs on — the one action that needs no permission, so it is also how a page proves the bridge works end to end.

caps.description: Capabilities THIS APK grants the page, read from its baked-in bridge.json. Without it a refusal is indistinguishable from a missing implementation.

installed.description: When this copy was installed or last updated — the only way to tell which build you are holding.

perms.description: Android permission -> held. What a tile needs to say full / partial / none honestly.

locationOn.description: Location services, device-wide. Off returns an EMPTY ble/wifi scan with no error — the most confusing failure in the whole bridge, because every permission still reads as granted.

actions.summary: Post a system notification. WebView has no Notification API at all, so this is the only way an app inside the shell can show one.

id.description: Reuse an id to REPLACE that notification rather than stack another.

ongoing.description: Not dismissable by swipe — for something actually in progress.

actions.summary: Dismiss a notification this app posted.

Fire a notification at a wall-clock time, offline, with the app closed — and again after a reboot. The web cannot do this at all since Notification Triggers was abandoned; it is the reason the APK exists.

id.description: Yours to choose; setting the same id again replaces that alarm.

at.description: Epoch milliseconds. In the past = fire now.

exact.description: False when the OS would only take an inexact alarm — Doze may shift it by minutes, and a screen that promises a time must say so.

actions.summary: Cancel a scheduled alarm.
Everything currently scheduled — the shell owns this state, so a reinstalled page can rediscover it.

Install an APK the page just built for this same app. The package name is a digest of the start URL, so it is an UPDATE of this app, never a second copy. Android always shows its own confirmation — a normal app cannot install silently, and pretending otherwise would be a lie.

base64.description: The APK bytes. The page fetched them; the shell never fetches.

actions.summary: Start a foreground service so work survives the screen going off. Android requires a persistent notification for it — that is the deal, and the user can always see what is running.

location.description: Also stream positions while it runs — needs background location.

actions.summary: Stop it. Nothing here holds a wakelock past this call.
Is it running, and since when — the shell owns this, so a reloaded page rediscovers it.
Positions while the app is closed. The web geolocation API stops the moment the page is backgrounded; this does not, which is the whole point.

Nearby networks. No web API exists for this in any browser. Android throttles scans hard (4 per 2 minutes in the foreground) and returns the LAST results when it refuses, so a caller must not read a repeat as movement.

caps.description: Security capabilities as the driver reports them.

ftm.description: is80211mcResponder — this AP answers a Wi-Fi RTT ranging request, which is the only REAL distance any radio on this phone can produce (Android documents 1-2 m). False on most home routers, so a screen must never offer ranging until a scan has said true.

std.description: getWifiStandard — 1 legacy, 4 11n, 5 11ac, 6 11ax, 8 11be. API 30+, absent below it.

width.description: channelWidth — 0 is 20MHz, 1 is 40, 2 is 80, 3 is 160, 4 is 80+80, 5 is 320. API 23+.

at.description: ScanResult.timestamp in microseconds since boot. A scan is a statement about WHEN; without it a throttled repeat is indistinguishable from a fresh look.

throttled.description: The OS refused a fresh scan; these are the previous results.

actions.summary: The connection this device is on, if any.
The cells this radio can see, serving one included. The web has nothing remotely like it — gsmscan has been guessing until now.

Ask Android for a runtime permission. Without it a capability can be granted to the page, compiled into the shell, and still refused forever — cell.info needs READ_PHONE_STATE and no web callback ever asks for it.

state.description: granted | denied — denied covers both a refusal and a permission the user has told Android to stop asking about.

actions.summary: Is there a Bluetooth radio, is it on, and what can it transmit. Web Bluetooth cannot answer any of this — it can only open a chooser.

advertising.description: Whether THIS app currently holds an advertisement in the air. The shell owns this state, so a reloaded page can find out instead of guessing.

extAdv.description: isLeExtendedAdvertisingSupported. Absent on a shell older than bridge 26 — which is how a page tells 'this controller cannot' apart from 'this shell cannot say'.

maxAdvLen.description: getLeMaximumAdvertisingDataLength — the controller's own ceiling, never assumed. 31 means legacy only; the HCI range tops out at 1650 and no phone owes you that.

multiAdv.description: isMultipleAdvertisementSupported. A boolean is all Android exposes — it is NOT a count, and treating it as one is how ADVERTISE_FAILED_TOO_MANY_ADVERTISERS arrives.

actions.summary: Every advertising device around you, as they appear. Web Bluetooth shows a chooser and returns the ONE device the user picks — it can never enumerate, which is exactly what a scanner needs.

started.description: Emitted once when startScan returned without throwing. Without it, a scan that never began and a scan that found nothing are the same empty screen.

ack.description: The bridge received the subscribe call, emitted before any logic runs — so a call that never arrived stops looking like one that was swallowed.

raw.description: The complete advertisement as lowercase hex. CANONICAL: a reduced schema cannot classify a protocol invented after this catalogue was written, and Android's own parser drops malformed structures. Absent on a shell older than bridge 24, which is how a page tells the difference between 'no payload' and 'this shell cannot send one'.

tx.description: Advertised transmit power in dBm (AD type 0x0A, or getTxPower on extended advertising). Absent means not advertised — it must NOT be defaulted, because an assumed reference power at 1 m is where an RSSI distance estimate becomes fiction.

tns.description: getTimestampNanos — monotonic since boot. Ordering and inter-advertisement intervals survive a wall-clock adjustment; `at` does not.

sid.description: Advertising SID, 0-15, extended advertising only. A fingerprint clue WITHIN one address epoch — never a durable identity.

dstat.description: getDataStatus — 0 complete, 1 truncated, 2 more-to-come. Parsing `raw` without checking this reads a fragment as a whole advertisement.

conn.description: Connectable. The non-owner GATT service (identify, play sound, disablement instructions) is only reachable when this is true.

actions.summary: Put bytes into the air for anyone nearby to hear. The peripheral role Web Bluetooth has never had — a browser can only ever be a central, so a phone running a page is invisible to every other phone. Non-connectable and non-discoverable: nothing can open a session against this device, and Android charges no 3-byte flags structure for it (BluetoothLeAdvertiser hasFlags = isConnectable && isDiscoverable), which is what leaves 27 usable bytes. Its own capability, deliberately: scanning and speaking are different powers and an app that reads the air must not be able to fill it.

data.description: Manufacturer-specific payload as lowercase hex, 1-27 bytes, carried under company id 0xFFFF (the SIG's internal/interoperability-test space — the shell fixes it so a page cannot impersonate a vendor). 31 legacy bytes minus AD length, AD type and the 2-byte company id is where 27 comes from.

more.description: A second payload of the same shape carried in the scan response, checked against its own 31-byte budget and never charged flags. Android forces legacy advertisements to be scannable and withholds the report until the scan response arrives, so this space is already paid for whether or not it is used.

ms.description: Stop by itself after this long. 0 holds it until ble.silence. The ceiling is the platform's, not ours: AdvertiseSettings.setTimeout THROWS above LIMITED_ADVERTISING_MAX_MILLIS (180 * 1000) rather than clamping, so a larger number would be an exception on the device and nothing in the air.

bytes.description: Payload bytes accepted, so a page can assert what actually went out rather than what it meant to send.

replaced.description: A previous advertisement was stopped to make room. One set at a time, the same way a second ble.scan replaces the first.

actions.summary: Stop transmitting. Named for the transmitter alone — a scan is stopped by dropping its subscription, and one verb that could mean either is one verb that eventually means the wrong one.

Assemble and broadcast one or more raw AD structures verbatim — arbitrary company id (manufacturer data) or 16-bit service UUID. The lab transmitter for studying proximity-pairing protocols (Apple Continuity, Fast Pair, Swift Pair, Eddystone) on your OWN devices. A separate capability from advertise, which stays locked to 0xFFFF so no ordinary app can wear a vendor's id; this one an app must list explicitly and gate behind consent. Non-connectable legacy by default; the assembled payload must fit the 31-byte legacy budget.

kind.description: manufacturer data (AD 0xFF, id is a company id) or service data (AD 0x16, id is a 16-bit UUID)

data.description: the AD value AFTER the id, lowercase hex. The assembled total across all structures must fit 31 legacy bytes; the shell rejects an over-budget set with the byte count.

connectable.description: default false; true costs the 3-byte AD flags structure out of the 31-byte budget

ms.description: auto-stop after this long; 0 holds until ble.silence. The ceiling is the platform's — AdvertiseSettings.setTimeout throws above it rather than clamping.

bytes.description: total assembled AD bytes that went out

replaced.description: a previous advertisement was stopped to make room — one set at a time

actions.summary: Attached USB devices. Needs no permission to ENUMERATE — unlike WebUSB, which cannot see a device until the user has picked it from a chooser.

Open and claim a USB device by vid/pid, asking the user once. Unlike WebUSB (which the WebView does not have) this works inside the app and can drive a vendor interface — it is how the native RTL8852AU driver reads registers.
A control transfer on the open USB device. IN (reqType 0xC0) returns hex; OUT (0x40) sends hex. This is the RTL8852AU vendor register read/write (request 0x05, wValue=addr[15:0], wIndex=addr[23:16]).

Mode-switch a mass-storage adapter to its wireless personality with a SCSI eject (START STOP UNIT). The RTL8852AU arrives as USB storage (0bda:1a2b) and must be ejected to re-enumerate as the Wi-Fi device (0b05:1997) before its registers exist.

A bulk transfer on the open USB device — OUT sends hex to an endpoint, IN reads up to length bytes. Carries firmware-download packets (EP 0x07) and received 802.11 frames (EP 0x84) for the full RTL8852AU bring-up.

Run a flat list of USB primitives on the open device in one native pass — control (c), bulk (b) and poll-until (p). The RTL8852AU bring-up is thousands of register writes and gated reads; one op per bridge call would be far too slow, so the app builds the op list and the shell executes it, returning only the reads by index.

Bring the already-open RTL8852AU (0b05:1997) on air in monitor mode: firmware download + captured-config replay + live IQK/TSSI/DPK calibration, run natively (the cal is adaptive, not a static op list). Requires a COLD chip — a warm one has degraded RX — so the app must have the user replug before this. After it succeeds, the app injects beacons on EP5 and reads EP0x84 through usb.bulk.
Release the native RTL8852AU libusb session opened by rf.attach (does not close the USB device — usb.close does that). Called when the mesh carrier stops.
The last lines the bridge wrote about its own behaviour. Every failure so far cost a reinstall to learn one bit, because the shell could report a result but never what it did on the way there.
Listen on the local network so other devices can open this phone. The one capability that is not about reading the device but about the device being REACHABLE — which a browser can never be.

url.description: The address another device can actually reach — the wifi one, not loopback.

actions.summary: Place one resource in memory for the server to hand out. The page supplies every byte; the shell never invents content, and there is no filesystem behind this.
Close the socket. Nothing keeps listening after this.
Where it is reachable and how many requests it has served.

Ask the user for a folder. This is why the capability needs no storage permission at all: the scope is what they picked, not what we claimed, and MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE — the one that hands over the whole device — is never declared.
Every folder already granted, kept across restarts — so a folder is chosen once rather than on every launch.
Children of one folder inside a granted tree. The page walks by passing back a docId a previous listing returned; it never builds a path itself.
One document's bytes, base64. Capped at 8MB because the whole body crosses the bridge in a single frame.
Create a file in a granted folder and fill it. A real save, to a place the user chose — not the Downloads dead-drop every browser is limited to.

Open an Android settings page for THIS app. The one exit from a permanently denied permission: once the user has said no twice, no dialog can ever appear again and a screen that only says "blocked" leaves them stranded.

Charge, charging state and whether the system is throttling this app. The Battery Status API was removed from every browser for fingerprinting; inside our own app there is no third party to leak it to.

unrestricted.description: Exempt from battery optimisation — the difference between a background service that survives the night and one Doze stops.

temp.description: Tenths of a degree C, as the OS reports it.

actions.summary: Hand something to another app through the system share sheet. WebView has no navigator.share at all, so this is the only way out of the app — and bytes go via MediaStore, which needs no permission and leaves the file where the user can find it again.

Who else is on this network. A browser has no raw sockets, no ARP and no way to probe an unknown host, so this exists nowhere on the web. FIVE independent sources, because ports alone found only the router on a real network: UDP to a closed port (the host answers ICMP unreachable — it proves itself BY refusing, which is how a firewalled laptop is found at all), /system/bin/ping (isReachable falls back to TCP port 7 and ignores its own timeout), a TCP connect sweep, and SSDP + mDNS multicast, whose replies identify a host by the address they come from. Reverse DNS names whatever answered.

name.description: Reverse DNS, or the SSDP SERVER line. Often absent — a bare address is an honest answer.

ports.description: Comma-separated open ports. EMPTY means it answered a ping but opened nothing, which is still a host.

via.description: udp | ping | tcp | ssdp | mdns — which source saw it. A host usually arrives more than once.

done.description: The sweep finished. A radio scan never does, so without this the list just stops growing and nothing says whether it is over.

progress.description: The sweep is partway through. Fifteen seconds of nothing reads as broken.

sources.description: Per-probe tally, e.g. tcp=1 udp=4 ping=6 ssdp=2 mdns=3. A bare host count cannot say WHICH probe is dead.

actions.summary: What is listening on this device itself. Android 10 closed /proc/net to apps, so nothing can ENUMERATE the listening sockets — the only way in is to connect to every port and see who answers, on 127.0.0.1 and ::1 both (an IPV6_V6ONLY listener is invisible to the IPv4 sweep). Identification is evidence, not a port table: listen first for a banner that identifies itself, ask HTTP only into silence, and try TLS on a fresh socket when the bytes are still unintelligible. Java returns the raw bytes; packages/runtime/portid.js decides what they mean, because a guess made in Java is a guess no gate can test. Needs no permission beyond INTERNET: loopback is outside Android's local-network definition.

ports.description: Comma-separated ports and inclusive ranges. Default is every port: a refused loopback connect is sub-millisecond, so the whole range costs seconds, and a curated list would only find what someone already expected.

ipv6.description: Sweep ::1 as well as 127.0.0.1. Both by default — they are different destinations.

identify.description: Run the probes. Off leaves a port list with nothing said about it.

family.description: 4 or 6 — WHERE it answered. A service on ::1 only is a different fact from one on 127.0.0.1.

probe.description: passive | http | tls | silent — which probe produced the bytes. Silence before we spoke is itself evidence.

hex.description: The captured bytes, lowercase hex, capped. The ONE evidence field: classification reads this, never a Java verdict.

tls.description: handshake_ok | alert | not_tls | timeout | io — transport outcome only, never a service name.

cert.description: Certificate subject, from a diagnostic trust-all handshake. What the service CLAIMS to be; it authenticates nothing.

gone.description: It accepted the sweep and refused the identification connection. Measured on a real box: two ports answered one sweep and refused the next, so a single connect is not proof that a service lives there.

progress.description: Partway through. 65k connects with nothing on screen reads as a hang.

done.description: The sweep finished. A sweep ENDS, unlike a radio scan, and must say so even at zero.

addrs.description: Which addresses were actually swept, comma separated. A phone with no ::1 sweeps one family, and a screen that assumed both would describe a sweep that never happened.

actions.summary: Post/update the OS media notification and own the framework MediaSession, so a page that is playing audio gets lock-screen transport and survives the screen going off. This is the shell POLYFILLING navigator.mediaSession, which browser-compat-data records as webview_android:false for every member (crbug 40611412) — a WebView is the one place a farm audio app has no media session at all, and it is also the only place where losing one kills the stream. Calling it again REPLACES the same notification, so the title tracks the track. It carries its own foreground service; bg.start is the generic one and the two are independent.

playing.description: PlaybackState STATE_PLAYING vs STATE_PAUSED. Without it System UI shows the wrong button and the lock screen argues with the app.

prev.description: Offer a previous action. A player with no queue must not show one.

actions.summary: Release the session and drop the notification with its foreground service. A session left behind is a phantom notification whose buttons reach nobody.

What the user pressed on the lock screen, in the notification, or on a headset — the return leg of the polyfill, standing in for MediaSession.setActionHandler. Without it the notification's buttons are decoration.

command.description: play | pause | next | prev | stop. `stop` is the user dismissing the player, not a transport press — a page that treats it as pause leaves a notification nobody asked for. Absent on an `ack` frame: a frame is one or the other.

ack.description: The bridge received the subscribe call. Without it a button that reached nobody looks exactly like a button nobody pressed.

actions.summary: Put this app in the system share sheet for the listed kinds, and take it out of every other. The manifest is baked per template, so the targets exist as DISABLED activity-aliases in every full shell and the page switches its own on — a farm of sixty APKs must not all answer 'share audio'. Persistent: PackageManager remembers the state across restarts and reboots.

kinds.description: audio = audio/* + application/ogg · image = image/* · video = video/* · text = text/plain · any = */*. An empty list withdraws from every sheet.
What is enabled now, as PackageManager reports it — not an echo of the request.

actions.summary: What another app shared INTO this one. A share that arrives before the page has subscribed (a cold start straight from the sheet) is held and delivered right after the ack, once; a share into a running app arrives as the next frame. Bytes cross as base64 in one frame, so an item is capped at 8MB like files.read.

ack.description: The bridge received the subscribe call. Absent on a share frame: a frame is one or the other.

mime.description: The intent's type, which is what the SENDER claimed — Telegram says audio/ogg for a voice note; a file manager may say application/octet-stream for the same bytes.

tooLarge.description: Over the 8MB cap: name, mime and size arrive, the bytes do not.

text.description: EXTRA_TEXT, when the sender attached or shared plain text.

actions.summary: Start the Godot engine UNDER the page with a project pack from the page's own origin. The shell's `godot` flavour carries Godot as a library (Vulkan Mobile, the camera through Godot's CameraServer); the page stays the UI on a transparent WebView. One engine per process: a second start replaces the pack.

pack.description: https URL of the .pck, on the page's origin. Cached by its bytes' digest.

params.description: Initial key/values handed to the project (the same as godot.set, before the first frame).

actions.summary: Stop rendering and release the camera; the engine stays loaded for the next start.
Hand one key/value to the running project (a preset, a knob, a mode) — the project's `MsPortal` singleton emits it as a signal.
A gesture on the stage, forwarded from the page — the WebView owns every touch, so the page relays what belongs to the picture: a tap (focus), a pinch (zoom), a pan.

scale.description: pinch: the factor since the pinch began.

actions.summary: The current frame as a PNG in Downloads (MediaStore), the way every save in the shell lands where the user can find it.
What the engine is doing: loading the pack, running (with the frame rate the project reports), stopped, or failed with a reason.
